A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
inhaled insulin is absorbed into systemic circulation from the lungs by passive diffusion, with the absorption being controlled by dose-dependent saturable metabolism in the lungs.

the lung kinetics of insulin are dominated by the balance between passive diffusion and saturable lung metabolism, and that the lung kinetics are not affected by the insulin dose, formulation, subject status (healthy vs diabetic) or inhalation manoeuvre, but may be affected by smoking status.
inhaled insulin is rapidly absorbed and cleared from the lung via passive diffusion and saturable metabolic clearance, respectively, with the absolute bioavailability being low (1.5%–4.8%).
The main takeaway from our work is that
the lung absorption of insulin is passive and dose-dependent, and that the rate of absorption can be controlled by deep inspiration.

the rate of insulin absorption in the lung is controlled by both passive diffusive absorption (i.e. the lung membrane permeability) and dose-dependent saturable metabolism (i.e. insulin-degrading enzyme activity) in the lung.

the lung metabolism, which is likely to be saturable, plays an important role in determining the disposition of inhaled insulin, and therefore, the lung kinetics and absorption efficiency are dose-dependent.
